newsitem.title: USA: Coffee hits 3-month low, grains and oil also fall.
newsitem.headline: Coffee hits 3-month low, grains and oil also fall.

text.p: Coffee prices fell on Thursday after a U.S. Agriculture Department official said a surprising estimate of the crop in top grower Brazil this week by one of the department's own analysts was probably too low.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange, coffee for September delivery closed down 15.35 cents a pound at 161.70 cents, its lowest price since April 10.

Prices backtracked from gains made after the department's attache in Brazil released his crop appraisal. The report, dated May 9 and published Tuesday on the Internet, put Brazil's crop now being harvested at 24 million 132-pound bags.
That assessment flew in the face of the department's own official estimate in June of 28 million bags for the Brazil crop, so the report sparked a sharp rally this week.

But a senior department official told Reuters late on Wednesday he had confidence in the earlier, 28 million bag estimate and that the attache's estimate did not take into account all factors influencing the crop.
"We stand by our numbers and the integrity of our system," said Ed Cissel, director of production estimates and crop assessment for the USDA's Foreign Agricultural Service.

"The attache reports come in from the field, and they are unofficial reports," Cissel said. "The information is evaluated here and the (USDA's) World Board evaluates the figures to make sure we come out with unbiased numbers.
"Our methodology is a convergence of evidence. We look at the attache reports, weather, statistical trends, trees planted and so forth," Cissel said.
Analysts said other factors also emerged to quell supply concerns, including rising warehouse stocks of coffee in the United States and continued mild winter weather in Brazil.
"Supply fears have dissipated," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast. "If you want coffee you can get it, and it is tempering any urge to go higher."
Grain prices also fell back as continued fine weather in the Midwest sparked selling by speculators.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, corn for July delivery closed down 2 cents a bushel at $2.47-3/4. July soybeans closed down 10 cents a bushel at $7.79 and July wheat closed down 4-1/4 cents a bushel at $3.21-1/2.
The National Weather Service said in its latest 6-to-10 day outlook that the Midwest would experience below-normal temperatures and above-normal rainfall from July 15 to 19.

That scenario would be nearly perfect for the U.S. corn crop, which is now entering its critical pollination or reproductive stage of development. This year's soybean crop is already expected at a record 2.6 billion bushels and the corn crop may rise as high as 10 billion bushels, the second biggest ever, according to government and private analysts.

Wheat prices were also pressured by excellent yields in the winter wheat crop now being harvested and by expectations that the Agriculture Department will raise its estimate for this year's winter wheat crop in a monthly report due on Friday.

At the New York Mercantile Exchnage, oil prices closed mostly lower after shrugging off news that Colombian rebels had dynamited a pipeline for the second time this week and forced a halt in oil production at the large Cano Limon field.
Traders focused instead on U.S. weekly oil industry data this week that showed plentiful and supplies of crude oil.
Crude for August delivery closed down 21 cents a barrel at $19.38.
Oil prices were pushed lower early on news that the German government expected to raise 400 million marks this year from oil reserve sales and would sell more oil in 1998.

August heating oil followed crude oil lower to close down 0.54 cent a gallon at 52.11 cents. Most gasoline contracts also fell but August gasoline ended up 0.37 cent a gallon at 58.60 cents, supported by jitters about a refinery fire.

Mobil Corp.'s Chalmette, Louisiana, refinery had a fire at its hydrocracking unit early on Thursday morning, but the fire lasted less than an hour. The unit, which converts middle distillates to high-octane gasoline, has a capacity of just under 20,000 barrels per day.
Mobil would not comment on whether units were idled by the fire.
